text: Every team that ships a service has the same argument eventually: engineering wants to move fast, someone else wants the thing to never go down, and without a number to anchor that fight, it never actually resolves. Site Reliability Engineering replaces that argument with math, using three connected ideas: the SLI, the SLO, and the error budget.

An SLI, a service level indicator, is one concrete, measured metric from the user's point of view — not server CPU, which is an internal health signal. Availability is successful requests over total requests. Latency is the percent of requests faster than some threshold. Durability and freshness cover stored data and pipelines. Every one of these is a ratio you can plot on a graph right now, not an opinion.

An SLO takes that SLI and draws a target on top of it, with a time window attached — ninety nine point nine percent over a rolling thirty days, for example. The error budget is just what's left: one hundred percent minus the SLO target. At ninety nine point nine percent over thirty days, that works out to roughly forty three minutes of allowed downtime. Tighten it to ninety nine point nine five, and the budget shrinks to about twenty one minutes.

The budget reframes reliability as something to spend deliberately. A team that hasn't touched its budget this month has real room to take risk — ship the big migration, try a faster release cadence. A team that's already burned most of it on an early outage should slow down and spend the rest of the month hardening instead. The data makes that call, so nobody has to argue about whether it feels safe enough to deploy.

That's also why one hundred percent is never the actual target: a service with zero error budget has zero room for the small risk every single deploy carries, which means it can't ship anything at all. Next lesson, we'll negotiate where that target should actually sit — balancing what users expect against what engineering can realistically deliver.
